prompt:
Could we mock up a basic DIY script to fetch one's own data from Google Health and send it to one's own Beeminder goal? I'm thinking something we could put in a repo in the Beeminder github org and people who were sufficiently tech savvy could fork it / copy it and cron it or whatever on their own machines. 

1. What are the token options -- I don't think Google does "personal auth token" stuff, so they may have to set up their own api client and do some oauth stuff? in which case it might need to be more than just a script that they can cron. but that's okay. it doesn't have to be accessible to everyone, but let's just keep the level of knowhow as low as possible, without costing ourselves support / dev time. 

2. want to use good beeminder-api hygiene -- use requestids for upsert where applicable, use diffsince and skinny params where appropriate, and even if the user decides to cron the script to run every 2 minutes, don't wind up with the integration sending 720 datapoints to the goal, that kind of thing.
reply:
Checked the Beeminder API docs locally (requestid upsert, diff_since/skinny). Next I'm looking up the current Google Health API auth story, then I'll write the script.

Google side is mostly mapped: each user makes their own Cloud project/OAuth client, and there's a 7-day refresh-token gotcha. Checking rate limits and the field names for a few more metrics now.

Found the exact rollup field shapes (e.g. `steps.countSum` is a string). Now checking Beeminder's server code, if it's checked out here, for how `create_all` reports duplicate requestids.

House Python style here is 2-space indents and terse. Writing the script now (stdlib only, no `requests`, so there's nothing to pip install).

Now the tests: stdlib `unittest`, with a fake HTTP layer standing in for both Google and Beeminder.

18/18 pass on Python 3.9 (macOS system python) and 3.12. Smoke-testing the CLI with a throwaway HOME so I don't touch your real `~/.config`:

The CLI behaves as expected. Last piece is DEVNOTES.md: design notes for you, plus the setup facts a README would need. I'm leaving the README itself for you to write, per the user-copy rule.

I've written a mockup in `googlefitbit/`. It's one Python script that needs nothing beyond Python 3.9+, so there's nothing to pip install. It passes 18 tests on Python 3.9 and 3.12, but only against faked APIs: nobody has run it on a real Google Health account yet.

- `beeminder_googlehealth.py`: run `setup` once (interactive), then cron the plain command at any frequency. `--dry-run` prints what it would send.
- `test_beeminder_googlehealth.py`: run with `python3 -m unittest`.
- `DEVNOTES.md`: design notes and open questions, plus the raw facts for a README. I left the README itself for you. Following CLAUDE.md, every message a user sees is a Russian placeholder marked `TODO:RUS`.

I didn't run `git init`, and nothing is staged.

## 1. Tokens

You're right: Google has no personal access tokens, so each user has to create their own OAuth client in Google Cloud. That turns out to be the good option:
- **If Beeminder shipped one shared client**, it would be Beeminder's app. All Google Health scopes are "Restricted", so going past 100 users means Google's verification plus a yearly outside security audit. That's the cost of the official integration, not of a DIY script.
- **With their own client**, each user is the only user of their own unverified app. Beeminder has no review to pass and no client to maintain.

Setup is about 15 minutes of clicking in the Google Cloud console, then a one-time browser consent where the user pastes back the URL they land on. That's the flow Google's own setup guide describes, so their docs match ours, and it also works over SSH on a headless machine. After that the script runs unattended on a refresh token.

The big gotcha: if the user leaves the app in "Testing" mode, the refresh token expires after 7 days. They have to click **Publish app**; it stays unverified and capped at 100 users, which is fine for one person. Skip that step and every user files a support ticket a week later. The script catches the expired token and tells them to rerun setup, but the README needs to make this step loud.

## 2. Beeminder API hygiene

- **One datapoint per goal per day.** The requestid is `googlehealth-<datatype>-<YYYYMMDD>`, sent through `create_all`, so a growing step count updates today's datapoint instead of adding a new one.
- **No Beeminder call when nothing changed.** A local cache remembers what was last sent for each day, and a run only posts days whose value changed. One test runs the sync 720 times with no new data and checks that it made exactly one Beeminder call (and one Google token refresh).
- **The cache is only a speed-up.** I checked the server code in `working-clones/b2`. Resending an identical datapoint comes back as a `"Duplicate request"` error with HTTP 200, and `create_all` skips the graph refresh when nothing changed. So the script treats those errors as success, and any other error fails loudly and gets retried on the next run.
- **Two server quirks the code works around:**
  - Comments are compared as `dp[:comment].to_s != dat.comment`, so a resend with no comment never counts as a duplicate (`"" != nil`). It would update and regraph every time. The script always sends the same non-empty comment.
  - If both are sent, `timestamp` overrides `daystamp`, so the script sends only `daystamp`. Google already splits days by the user's local calendar day.
- **I didn't use `diff_since`/`skinny`.** The sync never needs to read anything from Beeminder, and no read is cheaper than a skinny read. Where they'd help is noticing that someone edited or deleted the script's datapoints on the website. But the obvious check (watching the goal's `updated_at`) would also go off after the script's own writes trigger a graph refresh, and it costs a request every run to catch something rare. For now, such edits get overwritten only when that day's Google value next changes, or when the cache file is deleted. If you want the check anyway, it's easy to add.

## Needs a real run

- Whether Google really lets you publish an unverified app that uses restricted scopes. Their setup page implies yes.
- Whether the daily-total endpoint accepts a date range ending in the future. I query through tomorrow, in case the user's "today" is ahead of the cron machine's clock.
- The user must first sign in to the Google Health mobile app with the same Google account. Setup checks for this.

DEVNOTES.md also lists smaller limitations: night-owl deadlines, Active Zone Minutes left out, and a possible GitHub Actions version that needs no machine (but GitHub turns off scheduled jobs after 60 days of repo inactivity).

Sources:
- [About the Google Health API](https://developers.google.com/health/about)
- [Set up Google Cloud and OAuth](https://developers.google.com/health/setup)
- [dailyRollUp reference](https://developers.google.com/health/reference/rest/v4/users.dataTypes.dataPoints/dailyRollUp)
- [Aggregate data](https://developers.google.com/health/aggregate-data)
- [Endpoints](https://developers.google.com/health/endpoints)
- [Rate limits](https://developers.google.com/health/rate-limits)
- [App verification](https://developers.google.com/health/app-verification)

prompt: One datapoint per day is the right shape for things like steps, but for sleep it may not be -- how does google health handle sleep data? do they aggregate to one datapoint per day? if someone took a nap in the day does that get added into the total, or does it get added as an additional event? and what about activities -- does google health have activity data? e.g. runs. if a user recorded multiple runs in a day, that should probably translate to multiple datapoints recorded on beeminder for that day?
reply:
Looking up how the Google Health API models sleep and exercise.

No rollup value type exists for sleep or exercise, so neither has a daily total. Pulling the sleep and exercise schemas out of the reference page:

Sleep is session-based: each session has `metadata.nap`, `metadata.mainSleep`, and `summary.minutesAsleep`. Now the interval type and Exercise:

Sleep sessions are filtered by their civil *end* date (the morning you wake up), and exercise by civil start date. Both cap pages at 25. Checking `reconcile`, which list points sleep at:

Enough on the Google side. Before answering, I'll check how Beeminder's existing Fitbit autodata handles sleep and activities, since that's the precedent users will expect.

## Sleep

Google doesn't aggregate sleep to one per day. Each sleep is its own session data point, and a nap is a separate session, not added to the night. Each session carries:
- `summary.minutesAsleep` (also `minutesAwake`, `minutesInSleepPeriod`, and per-stage minutes), all as int64 strings.
- `metadata.nap`, true for short sleeps with no stages.
- `metadata.mainSleep`, marking the longest sleep with stages; there's one per day.
- A stable-looking `name` ID.
- `metadata.processed`, which is false while stages are still being computed. So `minutesAsleep` can change after we first see it, which the upsert already handles.

There's no daily total for sleep: `dailyRollUp` doesn't cover it, and the reference has no sleep rollup type at all. Grouping into days is up to us.

Which day a sleep belongs to: you can only filter sleep by end time, so it lands on the date you woke up. That's the old Fitbit `dateOfSleep` convention. "Tuesday's sleep" is Monday night plus any Tuesday nap. For sleep, `list` doesn't support filtering by data source and the docs send you to `reconcile`, which merges overlapping logs from different devices into one record.

**What Beeminder does today:** I checked `lib/fitbit.rb`. The `hours_slept` metric posts one datapoint per day, `summary.totalMinutesAsleep / 60` for that date. The old Fitbit summary added up every sleep log for the date, so naps are already counted in the total.

**My recommendation:** keep sleep in the per-day shape. Add up `minutesAsleep` across the sessions ending each day, convert to hours, and keep one requestid per day. That matches what current Fitbit users get. It also fixes itself when sessions get merged or split: Fitbit does split a night into two when you wake in the middle, and users edit sleeps. Per-session datapoints would leave orphans in those cases.

The real question is naps. "Sleep 7 hours a night" goals arguably shouldn't let a nap count. If you want that, I'd add it as a second metric (main sleep only) rather than a setting. Bedtime and wake-time metrics would only make sense for the main sleep anyway.

## Activities

Yes, the `exercise` data type exists. Each workout is its own data point with:
- `name`, an ID for the session.
- `exerciseType`, an enum of about 100 values (`RUNNING`, `WALKING`, `BIKING`, …).
- Civil start and end times.
- `activeDuration`, the duration excluding pauses.
- `metricsSummary`, with `distanceMillimeters`, `caloriesKcal`, `steps`, and average pace and speed.
- `dataSource.recordingMethod`: `MANUAL`, `ACTIVELY_MEASURED`, `PASSIVELY_MEASURED`, `DERIVED` or `UNKNOWN`.

There's no daily rollup for exercise either. You filter by civil start date, and a page holds at most 25 results, so the script needs paging. Fitbit's auto-detected walks can add up.

I agree that multiple runs should mean multiple datapoints, and Beeminder already has precedent. `lib/strava_goal.rb` posts one datapoint per activity, keyed by `strava_id`. It filters by activity type, uses a 7-day window, and the value is distance, duration, moving time, calories, or 1 for a count. (Beeminder's Fitbit "activities" metric goes the other way: one count per day.) In the script, the requestid would be built from Google's session ID, so each run upserts its own datapoint and a do-more goal sums them.

Caveats with sessions that daily totals don't have:
- **Orphans:** if someone deletes a duplicate or bogus auto-detected session in the Fitbit app, its Beeminder datapoint stays and inflates the total. The Strava integration has the same gap. Fixing it means storing the Beeminder datapoint ID from the `create_all` response in the cache, and deleting datapoints whose session disappeared within the window. That's destructive, and a glitch in Google's list (say, a paging bug) would delete real data, which the next run would then recreate. My lean is to match Strava for now and not delete.
- **ID stability:** whether these IDs stay the same between calls needs a real account to check. For raw `list` they should, since they're stored IDs. For `reconcile` the docs don't say. Raw `list` could count a run twice if two devices recorded it, so I'd start with `list` and check.
- **Dating:** I'd date a run by its civil start, since that's what Google filters on. Strava's integration uses end time, though a comment there points to issue #1810 about switching to start.

## Fit with the script

This is a small change: the cache and requestids would be keyed by requestid instead of by date. Per-day metrics (steps, sleep) use the date in the requestid, and session metrics use the session ID. Everything else stays: the 7-day window, sending only what changed, and treating duplicates as success.

## Three decisions for you before I build it

1. **Naps:** count them in the sleep total (what Fitbit users get today), or also offer a main-sleep-only metric?
2. **Deleted sessions:** match Strava and leave orphans, or delete datapoints whose session vanished?
3. **Exercise values:** which to offer? I'd suggest count, distance, and duration, with a list of exercise types per goal.

Sources:
- [Google Health sleep data type](https://developers.google.com/health/data-types/sleep)
- [Workouts data type](https://developers.google.com/health/data-types/workouts)
- [dataPoints reference (Sleep, Exercise, DataSource schemas)](https://developers.google.com/health/reference/rest/v4/users.dataTypes.dataPoints)
- [dataPoints.list (filters, 25-per-page cap)](https://developers.google.com/health/reference/rest/v4/users.dataTypes.dataPoints/list)
- [dataPoints.reconcile](https://developers.google.com/health/reference/rest/v4/users.dataTypes.dataPoints/reconcile)

reply:
I'll make sleeps (naps included) and workouts one datapoint per event, using Google's session ID as the requestid. Daily totals like steps stay one per day. The cache gets re-keyed by requestid so it works for both kinds. It's still only a speed-up: no orphan tracking, and nothing downstream depends on it.

Two spots came out too clever. Simplifying them:

Now the tests. The fake gains a paged `list` endpoint, and there are new cases for sleep, naps, multiple runs per day, and the type filter.

All 26 tests pass on Python 3.9 and 3.12. Updating DEVNOTES to match:

Each sleep, nap, and workout now becomes its own Beeminder datapoint. All 26 tests pass on Python 3.9 and 3.12, but still only against faked APIs. Nothing is staged.

**What changed**
- **Sleep:** the new `sleep_hours` metric gives one datapoint per session, worth `minutesAsleep`/60. Naps are their own sessions in Google, so they get their own datapoints. Each one lands on the day you woke up.
- **Workouts:** four new metrics, each one datapoint per workout, landing on the day it started:

  | Metric | Value |
  |---|---|
  | `exercise_count` | 1 |
  | `exercise_km`, `exercise_mi` | distance |
  | `exercise_hours` | `activeDuration`, so pauses don't count |

  Each workout's comment starts with Google's own label (e.g. "Running, …") so two same-day runs can be told apart.
- **Picking workout types:** in setup, an exercise goal is a line like `run exercise_km RUNNING TRAIL_RUNNING`. Types must be Google's exact enum names in capitals; lowercase is rejected. A goal with no types counts every workout.
- **Requestids:** for sleeps and workouts it's `googlehealth-<datatype>-<Google's ID for that event>`. Daily totals (steps, floors, distance, weight) are unchanged: one datapoint per day.
- **Cache:** it's now keyed by requestid instead of by day. It's still only there to skip Beeminder calls when nothing changed; deleting it just causes a resend.
- **Orphans:** a session deleted in the app leaves its Beeminder datapoint alone. There's no cleanup code.
- **Setup:** asks for the sleep scope only if a goal uses sleep. Workouts use the activity scope steps already need.

**To check on a real account**
- **Event IDs have to stay the same between calls.** If they don't, every run creates new datapoints. I read from Google's plain `list` endpoint, which returns stored IDs. The other endpoint (`reconcile`) merges data from multiple devices, but its docs don't say whether its IDs are stable. The catch with `list`: someone wearing a Pixel Watch and a Fitbit to bed might get the same sleep twice.
- **Two optional fields are required by the script.** These are a workout's `activeDuration` and a sleep's `summary`; without them the script fails loudly. If Google leaves out `summary` while it's still processing a night's sleep, sync would error every run until processing finishes.

Weight still sends one daily average, though each weigh-in is an event too. You only asked for sleep and workouts, so I left it; switching it to one datapoint per weigh-in would be a small change. DEVNOTES.md now covers all of this, plus the sleep scope and the type-name format for the README.

reply:
Checking how Google shapes individual weigh-ins: the sample time format, and whether weight data points have an ID like sleeps and workouts do.

Now the tests:

28/28 pass on 3.9 and 3.12, and no stale references remain. Updating DEVNOTES:

- **Value and date:** each datapoint is `weightGrams` converted to kg or lb. It's dated by the local day of the weigh-in.

- **IDs:** each weigh-in has its own ID in Google's API, so the requestid is `googlehealth-weight-<id>`, like sleeps and workouts. Google's docs say weight supports get, update and delete, which is why I expect those IDs to exist. That's the same unconfirmed point already in DEVNOTES: the IDs need to stay stable between calls, which needs a real account to check.

Steps, floors and distance are now the only metrics still sent as one daily total. DEVNOTES.md is updated to match.

reply:
The README is user-facing, but you've asked for it in English, so I'll write real copy instead of Russian placeholders. First I'm re-reading DEVNOTES.md, which changed on disk, and checking the exercise-type names and the reference-page anchor I plan to link.

Confirmed: that page returns `{"username": …, "auth_token": …}`. Writing the README:

prompt: ok, i'm stepping through the instructions in the readme. i got to "2e. Add yourself as a user, then publish", but publishing is still disabled -- it says "To publish your app you must complete your configuration on the Branding Page". When google makes the logins of test accounts expire after 7 days, are they not refreshable using a refresh token?
reply:
Checking what the Branding page requires before Google allows publishing:

Short answer: no. In Testing mode it's the refresh token itself that expires, so it can't be refreshed. And I got step 2e wrong: publishing needs more Branding fields than the README asks for.

**Why Testing mode breaks after 7 days.** Google issues two tokens:
- An **access token** lasts about an hour. The script gets a new one automatically from the refresh token, and that part keeps working.
- The **refresh token** has a fixed lifetime. In Testing it expires 7 days after it was issued, no matter how often it's used. Google's docs: a Testing-status project "is issued a refresh token expiring in 7 days," unless the only permissions requested are basic profile info.

After 7 days Google rejects the refresh token (`invalid_grant`), and the only fix is a fresh browser consent, which means re-running setup. Once the app is published, the refresh token has no fixed expiry. It only dies if it's revoked or goes unused for six months. So for anyone running this on cron, publishing is effectively required.

**Getting Publish enabled.** Google's Branding help page says the **App domain** links (home page, privacy policy, terms of service) "are required for all external production apps." The domains of those links also go under **Authorized domains**. My README only covers app name and support email, so that's the gap.

What I don't know is whether Google checks that you *own* those domains when you publish, or only when you apply for verification. The help page ties ownership checks to verification and doesn't say they block publishing. Since you're in the console now, you could try this:

1. On the Branding page, fill in **App domain** with the repo's GitHub URL for all three links (home page, privacy policy, terms of service). Any public page will do for this test.
2. Add `github.com` under **Authorized domains**, and save.
3. Go back to Audience and see whether **Publish app** is enabled.

If that works, I'll update step 2e of the README and add a short Privacy section that the privacy-policy link can point to. If Google insists on a domain you own, that's a much bigger barrier for DIY users. Let me know which way it goes, and I'll update the README (which I see you've been editing) to match.

Sources:
- [Manage OAuth App Branding (Google Cloud Help)](https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/15549049)
- [Using OAuth 2.0 to Access Google APIs: refresh token expiration](https://developers.google.com/identity/protocols/oauth2)

prompt: ok, so i entered some pages on my personal website for the URL and privacy policy links and publish is now enabled. it wouldn't let me save without also adding an "authorized domain", so i also used my bsoule.com domain for that, which it was happy with, though I'm concerned this might fux up the setup / get-a-token step down the line...
reply:
The `bsoule.com` entry won't break the token step. What could cause trouble is the redirect address: `https://www.google.com` may need `google.com` on that same list.

**What the list does.** Authorized domains is an allowlist of where your app's links and redirects are allowed to point. Google checks it when you save settings in the console. The login itself happens on `accounts.google.com`, and the script trades the code for tokens with `oauth2.googleapis.com`. Neither step looks at your authorized domains.

**What might bite at step 2f.** Google's Branding help page says: "All domains used in your project, whether in the branding page or client configuration pages must be pre-registered here," and "Add your Authorized Domains before you add your redirect or origin URIs." The client's redirect address is `https://www.google.com`, so `google.com` probably needs to be on the list too. Google's own Health setup guide tells you to use that address, but it assumes Testing mode, where this check may not apply.

**What I'd try next:**
1. On the Branding page, add `google.com` as a second authorized domain, next to `bsoule.com`, and save.
2. Then do 2f as written.

If Google accepts `google.com`, that also tells us the list doesn't require owning the domain. Then the README can tell people without a website to use their fork's GitHub URLs for the home page and privacy links, with `github.com` as the authorized domain. I can't confirm that inference, but it would be a strong hint. If Google refuses `google.com`, the fallback is a "Desktop app" client. Those redirect to `http://127.0.0.1`, which as far as I know skips the domain check. You'd copy the address from the browser's "can't connect" page instead of from google.com, which works just as well over SSH. That needs a small script change.

The README needs updating either way. Step 2c currently asks only for the app name and support email. It should also cover home page and privacy-policy links, plus authorized domains, added before the client is created. Tell me how `google.com` goes and I'll write it up to match. I'll wait so I don't collide with your edits.

Sources:
- [Manage OAuth App Branding (Google Cloud Help)](https://support.google.com/cloud/answer/15549049)
- [Matomo forum: Google OAuth client config setup issue](https://forum.matomo.org/t/google-oauth-client-config-setup-issue/30832)
- [Google dev forum: "must use a domain that is a valid top private domain"](https://discuss.google.dev/t/oauth-unable-to-use-aws-ec2-instance-for-authorized-redirect-uris/125013)

Neither: it's one fixed folder in your home directory, `~/.config/beeminder-googlehealth/`. For you that's `/Users/bsoule/.config/beeminder-googlehealth/`. It's the same no matter where the script lives, because the script hard-codes that location. It doesn't look in its own directory or mirror the script's path.

It sits outside the script's directory on purpose. That directory is a git checkout, and keeping your client secret, refresh token and Beeminder token out of it means a stray `git add .` can't commit them. `~/.config/<tool name>/` is the usual Unix place for a command-line tool's per-user settings.

Moving the JSON file there is only a suggestion, so you know where it is the next time you run setup. Setup asks for the file's path, so it can live anywhere. Setup also creates the folder itself.

"The script's config folder" was ambiguous, so I've reworded the end of 2f. It now says the folder is fixed in your home directory regardless of where the script is, says why, and says that moving the file there is optional.
